questions.question: Which statement is a key consequence involving compact sets?
options: The continuous image of a compact set is compact.
The continuous image of any set is compact.
Every compact set is open.
Every bounded set is compact in every metric space.

questions.question: Which operation on compact sets is guaranteed to preserve compactness?
options: Finite unions of compact sets.
Arbitrary unions of compact sets.
Complements of compact sets.
Images under arbitrary functions.

questions.question: Which subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not compact?
options: $\left\{(x,y)\colon 0\le\dfrac{x}{y}\le10,\ y\neq0\right\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2\colon 0<x^2+y^2<5\}$

questions.question: Which misuse of Heine-Borel is ruled out by the Euclidean-space hypothesis?
options: Assuming a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact without checking closedness.
Assuming closed and bounded implies compact in every metric space.
Assuming a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact without checking boundedness.
Assuming compact implies closed and bounded in every metric space.

questions.question: Which statement correctly combines Heine-Borel with the extreme value theorem mentioned?
options: Every function on a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ attains extrema.
Every continuous real-valued function on an open and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ attains its extrema there.
A continuous real-valued function on a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ attains extrema.
A closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ must contain only finitely many points.

questions.question: Which subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact by Heine-Borel?
options: $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Which property fails for $[0,+\infty)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ to be compact by Heine-Borel?
options: Closedness.
Boundedness.
Being a subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
Having real points.

questions.question: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. What does the Heine-Borel theorem say about $E$?
options: $E$ is compact if and only if it is closed.
$E$ is compact if and only if it is bounded.
$E$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
$E$ is compact if and only if it is open and bounded.

questions.question: Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which of the following sets need not be compact?
options: $K_1\cup K_2$
$K_1\cap K_2$
$K_1\setminus K_2$
$K_1\cup\{\boldsymbol{p}\}$ for a point $\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^n$

questions.question: The open intervals $(1/n,1)$, $n\ge2$, cover $(0,1)$. Why does this cover show that $(0,1)$ is not compact?
options: Any finite subfamily covers only $(1/N,1)$ for its largest $N$, so it misses $(0,1/N]$.
A cover by infinitely many open sets already shows that the set is not compact.
The point $0$ must be covered, and no interval $(1/n,1)$ contains $0$.
Each $(1/n,1)$ is not compact, and a union of non-compact sets is never compact.
